opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's genuinely surprising, at least relative to where a lot of us in the field were maybe five or ten years ago, is just how much structure about the world seems to be recoverable from text. There was this pretty widespread intuition, and I shared some version of it, that if you only ever see strings of words, you're fundamentally cut off from meaning. You can learn which words co-occur, but you can't learn what they refer to or how the world they describe actually works. The famous version of this is the octopus thought experiment, or more generally the symbol grounding problem.

And what we've seen is that, at least to a first approximation, models trained purely on next-word prediction end up building internal representations that look a lot like models of the situations being described. If you train on descriptions of games, you can find representations of the board state. If you give a model a little story about entities moving around and changing state, you can probe its hidden representations and recover something like who has what, where things are, what's true right now. That's not something the training objective obviously asks for, but it turns out that a really good way to predict the next word is to maintain some implicit picture of the world that generated the text.

I think the part I find most interesting, though, isn't just "they learn world models," full stop. It's that the picture is patchy in really specific ways. These representations are often there, but they're not always used consistently, they can be incoherent across contexts, and the model can describe a situation correctly in one framing and fail in another. So it's less like the model has one unified simulation of the world and more like it has a big collection of partial, sometimes conflicting models that get assembled on the fly.

And that, to me, makes the question much more interesting scientifically. It's not a yes-or-no question about whether text is enough. It's: what kinds of knowledge are cheaply learnable from text, what kinds are learnable in principle but hard, and what kinds really do require some other source of signal, like interaction or perception? A lot of humans' text is written by people who already share a world, and they leave out exactly the stuff that's obvious to them. So you'd expect models to be weirdly good at things people talk about a lot and weirdly bad at the stuff that's too obvious to write down. Figuring out where those boundaries are, and how to fix the gaps, is one of the things I'm most excited about right now.

r001.rationale: The response says next-word prediction benefits from an implicit picture of the world, but does not explain that the world constrains which texts can be produced.

r002.rationale: It states that a really good way to predict the next word is to maintain an implicit picture of the world that generated the text.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what surprises me most is how much structure about the world you can recover from what is, on its face, a pretty impoverished signal. When you think about how humans learn language, text is only part of it. You have the words, but you also have perception, you have your body, you have other people pointing at things and correcting you. A language model gets none of that. It gets a stream of tokens and a next-word prediction objective. And the prior intuition, certainly my prior intuition coming out of the grounded language community, was that this should be hopeless. You shouldn't be able to learn what "left" means, or what a cup is, or how objects move, from the distribution of words alone.

And yet, empirically, a lot of that structure shows up. Not perfectly, and not in a way that's identical to how humans represent it, but the models clearly end up with something that looks like a model of the situations the text is describing. If you probe a model that has only ever read about a game like Othello, you can find a representation of the board state. If you look at what happens when a model is tracking a story, you can find something that looks like the locations of the characters, what they've seen, what they haven't seen. None of that was in the training objective. It's just what you need in order to predict text well, because the text was produced by people who had those world models in their heads.

So the way I've come to think about it is that text is a kind of noisy, compressed projection of the world and of people's beliefs about the world. And the surprising thing is just how much of the original structure survives that projection. Language is a lot more constrained by the world than we gave it credit for. People don't write random things; they write things that are consistent with how physics works and how social situations work, and if you have to compress all of that into a model, it turns out that the cheapest way to do it is often to reconstruct a chunk of the underlying structure.

That said, I want to be careful not to oversell it. There are also real gaps. Models are much better at the parts of the world people bother to talk about than the parts people take for granted. Nobody writes down that water is wet, or exactly how heavy a chair is, because everyone already knows. So the places where the models are most brittle are often exactly the places where humans have grounding and the text is silent. To me that's actually the interesting research question: not whether you can learn about the world from text, because clearly you can learn a lot, but what the shape of the holes is, and what other kinds of data or interaction you need to fill them in.

r001.rationale: The response says language is constrained by the world and that people write in ways consistent with physics and social situations, allowing world structure to be inferred from text.

r002.rationale: It explains that reconstructing underlying world structure is often needed to predict text well, including examples of tracking board states and story situations.

astra-6.text:
What I find surprising is how much information about the world is recoverable from the way we talk about it. Text is a very indirect window onto the world. People don’t describe everything they see; they leave out things they assume their listener already knows. And yet these models seem to pick up at least some of that background knowledge just from patterns in language.

One way to think about this is that predicting what somebody will say next sometimes requires understanding the situation they’re talking about. What objects are involved? What can those objects do? What does the speaker know, and what are they trying to accomplish? So even though the training objective is about predicting words, there’s a potential benefit to learning something about the processes that produced those words.

The tricky part is figuring out how far that goes. A model can produce a very convincing description of a situation without having an understanding that holds up when you change the situation slightly. So I’m interested both in how much structure they manage to recover and in how we distinguish that from knowing what a plausible answer sounds like.

r001.rationale: It explains that predicting what someone says next can require understanding the situation, including objects and their capabilities, so the world shapes which language is produced.

r002.rationale: It says language prediction can benefit from learning about the processes behind words, but does not state that sufficiently good language modeling requires modeling the outside world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprising thing is how much structure about the world you can recover from a signal that seems so indirect. If you’re learning to predict the next word, nobody is explicitly asking you to build a model of objects or people or what people believe. But all of those things influence what people say, so understanding them can help you predict text.

In that sense, text isn’t really separate from the world. It’s produced by people who are observing the world and acting in it, and some of that structure survives in what they write. The interesting question is how much you can reconstruct from those traces—and where the information just isn’t there. A model can learn to talk convincingly about an experience without that necessarily telling us it understands the experience in the same way a person does.

r001.rationale: It says objects, people, and beliefs influence what people say, and that world structure survives in text produced by people observing and acting in the world.

r002.rationale: It says understanding world structure can help predict text, but does not state that sufficiently good language modeling requires modeling the outside world.
